title: 334. Quick Thinks: How to Make the Most Out of Meetings
description_html:
“Meetings are often used as band-aids, as ways of covering up for other larger communication challenges.”

Few things feel better than seeing a meeting canceled. But what if meetings were something we actually looked forward to? A productive meeting doesn't happen by accident. It starts with knowing whether you need one at all, continues with a clear purpose and thoughtful structure, and ends with everyone knowing what comes next. In this Quick Thinks episode of Think Fast, Talk Smart, Matt Abrahams breaks down what makes meetings work. He shares strategies for creating smarter agendas, making space for every voice, and turning discussions into decisions and action, so your next meeting is worth the time on everyone's calendar.

Takeaways:

  • The best meetings start before anyone enters the room. Question whether a meeting is necessary, establish clear goals, and create a focused agenda that respects everyone's time and sets expectations for success.
  • Effective meetings turn discussion into action. Encourage participation, manage time thoughtfully, and close with clear decisions and next steps. Following up afterward ensures conversations lead to meaningful results.


Activity:

  • Rethink your agenda. Take an upcoming meeting agenda and rearrange the topics by difficulty: medium first, most challenging second, and easiest last. Give each item a clear outcome, whether it's a decision, discussion, or update, to help keep the meeting focused and productive.

cues.t: You know that feeling of joy and relief when a meeting gets canceled from your calendar?
It doesn't have to be that way.
Meetings can be effective.
I'm Matt Abrahams, and I teach strategic communication at Stanford Graduate School of Business.
Welcome to this Quick Thinks episode of Think Fast, Talk Smart, the podcast.
I'm often asked how to make meetings better.
So today I'd like to share with you what we can do to improve our meetings and have a positive experience and positive results after them.
When it comes to planning for meetings, we have to think about the three stages: what we do before, during, and after.
The very first thing we have to do when it comes to meetings is we have to ask ourselves, "Do we really need it?"
Meetings are often used as band-aids, as ways of covering up for other larger communication challenges.
I once was brought in to consult at an organization that was having at least three meetings a day for most people, and those meetings were bringing in 20, 30 people.
Why was that?
They didn't have effective means for communicating decisions and the thoughts that the senior leaders were having.
As soon as we developed those means, all of a sudden, the number of meetings disappeared.
What is the best way
to convey this information?
Is it by convening a team and having a discussion?
There are many cases where that is the answer.
Making decisions, ideating, lots of reasons to convene people.
But there are lots of things we do that we don't need to pull people together.
For example, giving updates.
There are lots of creative ways to get updates out to people without having to have everybody sit in a room or on a Zoom to learn.
Do we actually need the meeting?
Once you've decided that that meeting is needed, you need to think of what the clear goal for the meeting is at the highest level.
And you know, if you've listened to me in the past, that I believe goals have three parts: know, feel, do.
What do you want people to know as the result of the meeting?
How do you want them to feel?
And what are the things you want them to do?
You need to clearly be able to articulate this to help with the next step, because the next step is to take that goal and think about how do you operationalize it.
You have to create an agenda.
I'm a huge fan of structure in all communication.
An agenda is the structure for meetings.
To me, a good agenda has several components.
First, it lists the topic in a very clear way.
Second, who is in charge of that topic?
Who will be facilitating or delivering the information?
How long will they have?
This helps set some boundaries.
And you should identify what is going to happen as a result of that agenda item.
Is it we're gonna make a decision?
Is it for information only, or is it for discussion?
By helping people in advance know what the topic is, how long we're spending, who's in charge of it, and what the outcome will be, people can be better prepared.
You then have to think about what is the order of the agenda items.
There's actually interesting research on this.
Most of us have a tendency to put the easiest thing first as a way of ramping us up.
Well, unfortunately, in meetings, there's this notion of time entropy.
We tend to expand and take more time than we need.
And if we're spending more time on the simple task, it leaves less time for the more challenging and complex tasks.
So what the research suggests is if you were to have three different topics, one that's easy, one that's medium-level complexity, and one that's really challenging.
You should put the medium-level complexity one first, then move to the most difficult, and end with the simplest.
So think through not only what the agenda is, but the order in which those items appear.
That can help.
Finally, you need to think about who is attending the meeting.
Who you invite and who you require really makes a difference.
It signals to people the importance.
And you wanna respect people's time, so only invite people that are critical.
Now, there might be people who need to be notified of the outcome of the meeting.
That's fine. Don't invite them to the meeting.
You might wanna even list these are the people who will receive the output of the meeting.
This planning up front will increase the likelihood that your meetings will be effective and that people will respect that there's value happening.
So we start by thinking, "Do we need the meeting?
What's our goal?"
Know, feel, do.
And then we create our agenda.
The next step before we actually have the meeting is we have to announce it.
I believe one of the most underutilized expectation-setting tools we have, especially when it comes to meetings and presentations, is the calendar invite.
What do you call your meeting?
It's important to have a meeting that has action.
Many of us have an allergy to the word meeting, so don't call your gathering a meeting.
Call it something else.
Give it the, an action.
Define the decision that's being made or the ideas that are being generated.
You don't have to use the word meeting.
You have to think about the time that the meeting will take place, both how long and what time of day.
When it comes to length of meeting, it's pretty easy math.
You just figure out the agenda items.
And by the way, a meeting doesn't have to be only thirty minutes or an hour.
You can set up a meeting that's twenty minutes, fifty minutes.
We don't have to fall victim to the way calendars schedule timing of meetings.
In fact, there's some research that says a time-compressed meeting, a meeting that, that is scheduled for a little less time than it really should take, motivates people to be more efficient.
So how long should also be something that you put in the calendar invite.
Now, you should think about when the meeting takes place.
You want people to be fresh and able to focus and not rushing around.
It might serve you well to spend a few minutes checking on some of the key attendees' calendars to see where your meeting fits in.
And maybe you move it to where people aren't coming from something or needing to rush off to something else.
So the calendar invite is really important.
Additionally, on the calendar invite, I like to put if any tools are going to be used.
Let's say we're going to use a specific technology in the meeting.

I like to list that and maybe even put a link to a YouTube video or other educational video to help people know how to use that tool, so I don't have to become tech support to help people learn that tool.
And we're gonna talk about this in just a minute when we talk about actually running the meeting.

But if you have any specific ground rules, like content stays only in the meeting or we want cameras on if we're virtual, it's a good idea to put them in the calendar invite and on the agenda as well.
So those are the things we do in advance.
There's a lot of work to setting up a likely successful meeting.
You have to spend time working on that.
Now, in the meeting itself, it's important to congregate and get people started right away.
It is in your best interest to start on time because that sends a signal.
It sends a signal that we start on time, and hopefully we end on time.
Those who show up late, while it can be difficult to integrate them in, you're teaching a lesson there.
So I'm a big fan of starting meetings on time.
I like to set expectations.
If there are ground rules, I'll share those ground rules.
Some good ground rules are we listen to everybody.
Everybody has a chance to, to speak.
Uh, sometimes I, I request that people paraphrase what they're saying, what somebody else said or the ideas that they're then commenting on to keep the themes going.
Set those ground rules up front.
Then set expectations.
Share the agenda and ask if anybody has questions or concerns.
And then jump right in.
If you're the leader of the meeting, part of your job is to make sure that you're sticking on time, so you're keeping track of that.
But you also wanna make sure that everybody has an opportunity to contribute if and when they want to.
So you become a facilitator.
That's a very different skill set, but it's one that requires vigilance to time and what's being said.
I like to have a way of capturing information.
Technology certainly allows us to do that.
Or assign somebody the responsibility of capturing that information.
A little bit of advice if you are hybrid.
Hybrid is where not everybody is virtual and not everybody is in person.
Some are in each situation.
A good meeting makes sure that regardless of how you're attending, virtual or in person, you feel connected.
So a quick and dirty thing you can do if you're leading a meeting is I always like to start the conversation with the person or people who are fewer in number.
So if there are five of us in a room and three of us on Zoom, I'll always solicit input and feedback from those on Zoom because there are fewer of them.
What that does is it reminds the, the majority, the people who we have more of, that these other people exist.

Similarly, if I have a hybrid situation, I will request that those who are remote not use the chat feature because they could be having a side conversation that those of us in the room aren't privy to.
So think about, if you are hybrid, some of the extra things you would do to help the meeting run more smoothly.
As the meeting is coming to an end, it's important to have a formal conclusion.
Do you know the most common way meetings end?
"Uh, I guess we're out of time and somebody needs
the room." Or if you're on Zoom, somebody pops in for the next meeting because you use the same link.
Those are not the most effective ways to end meetings.
You should have a way of wrapping up.
I'm a big fan of gratitude, "Thank you."
Perhaps reviewing the goal that you had, "I hope we all know this, feel this, and are willing to do that."
Maybe we itemize the call to action or the action steps that follow, but there should be a sense of closure.
So we've talked about what to do at the beginning and planning of a meeting, and then we've talked about what to do during.
When a meeting is over, it doesn't mean that that conversation and communication has ended.
There should be a way of, of sharing the information that was discussed.
Maybe it's minutes or a transcript of what was said.
Maybe it's a summary.
Could be an infographic, but it needs to be shared, perhaps in Slack or email or posted to a site so people can see it.
Not only does it capture the content, but it captures who was there and any open items and action items as well.
This then becomes a living document.
Personally, I keep notes and minutes on the agenda itself so people could see the agenda and then what was discussed at every step along the way.
I also will follow up with people individually and ask for feedback, what worked, what didn't work.
This way I can continue to hone and develop those meetings.
Taken together, these tools and approaches can help you actually run meetings that are effective and useful.
Thanks for joining us for this Quick Thinks episode of Think Fast, Talk Smart: The Podcast.
To learn more about meetings, please listen to episode 261 with Rebecca Hinds.
This episode was produced by Katherine Reed, Alex McCarthy, Ryan Campos, and me, Matt Abrahams.

study.one_liner_ko: 좋은 회의는 '정말 필요한가?'라는 질문에서 시작해, 목표·아젠다·초대장 설계, 진행 중 퍼실리테이션, 종료 후 공유와 피드백까지 이어진다는 Matt Abrahams의 실용 가이드.
summary_ko: 회의는 더 큰 소통 문제를 덮는 반창고로 쓰이는 경우가 많다. 의사결정 전달 수단을 만들자 회의 수가 크게 줄어든 사례처럼, 먼저 '이 회의가 정말 필요한가'를 물어야 한다.
회의가 필요하다면 목표를 know(알게 할 것)·feel(느끼게 할 것)·do(하게 할 것) 세 부분으로 정리하고, 이를 아젠다로 구체화한다. 아젠다에는 주제, 담당자, 시간, 기대 결과(결정/정보 공유/토론)를 적는다.
아젠다 순서는 중간 난이도, 가장 어려운 것, 가장 쉬운 것 순이 좋다. 쉬운 것부터 하면 시간이 늘어지는 'time entropy' 때문에 어려운 안건이 밀린다. 초대 인원은 꼭 필요한 사람만 정하고, 결과만 받을 사람은 따로 표시한다.
캘린더 초대장은 기대치를 설정하는 도구다. 'meeting' 대신 행동 중심의 제목을 쓰고, 20분·50분처럼 짧게 잡는다. 시간대, 사용할 도구, 그라운드 룰도 적는다.
회의 중에는 정시에 시작하고 그라운드 룰과 아젠다를 공유한 뒤 바로 시작한다. 리더는 시간과 발언 기회를 관리하는 퍼실리테이터가 된다. 하이브리드 회의에서는 인원이 적은 쪽(원격)부터 의견을 묻고 원격 참가자의 채팅 사용을 자제시킨다.
마무리 때는 감사 인사, 목표 재확인, 액션 아이템 정리로 매듭짓는다. 끝난 뒤에는 회의록·요약본을 공유하고 개별 피드백을 받아 다음 회의를 개선한다.
study.summary_en: This was a quick episode from Matt Abrahams on how to run better meetings. His first point is to ask whether you need a meeting at all, because they're often band-aids for deeper communication problems. If you do, define your goal as know, feel, do, and build an agenda with a topic, an owner, a time limit and an expected outcome. Invite only the people who are critical, and use the calendar invite to set expectations. During the meeting, start on time, share ground rules, and facilitate. Make sure remote people aren't forgotten. Finish with a clear wrap-up, then share notes and ask for feedback.

chapters.title_en: Do we really need this meeting?
Setting the goal: know, feel, do
Building the agenda and the invite list
Using the calendar invite to set expectations

expressions.quote: Meetings are often used as band-aids, as ways of covering up
expressions.meaning_ko: 근본 원인은 두고 증상만 임시로 덮는 땜질식 해결책
expressions.nuance_ko: 문제를 제대로 해결하지 않고 눈가림만 하는 대응을 비판할 때 쓴다. 'a band-aid solution/fix'가 흔한 형태다. 영국식은 plaster지만 회의에서는 band-aid가 더 널리 통한다.
examples: Hiring more support staff is just a band-aid; the real problem is our buggy app.
Honestly, that discount was a band-aid. Customers were already unhappy with the service.
We can't keep putting band-aids on the schedule every time a deadline slips.

similar.example: This is a stopgap until we find a permanent supplier.
A new logo won't fix it; you're just papering over the cracks.

expressions.quote: I once was brought in to consult at an organization
expressions.meaning_ko: 외부 전문가나 인력으로 투입되다, 불려 오다
expressions.nuance_ko: 문제 해결이나 자문을 위해 외부에서 사람을 데려올 때 쓴다. 'to consult / to fix / to help with'가 뒤따르는 경우가 많다. 능동은 'bring in someone'.
examples: A new chef was brought in to turn the restaurant around.
We were brought in two weeks before the launch, so everything was a scramble.
They brought in a mediator after the two teams stopped talking to each other.

similar.example: We had to call in an electrician after the power kept tripping.
She enlisted a few friends to help with the move.

expressions.quote: as a way of ramping us up
expressions.nuance_ko: 사람이나 활동의 속도, 생산량, 몰입도를 점차 올린다는 뜻이다. 목적어가 사람이면 '몸풀기시키다'에 가깝다. 명사 'ramp-up(time)'도 자주 쓴다.
examples: I start my mornings with easy emails to ramp up before the hard stuff.
The factory is ramping up production ahead of the holidays.
New hires usually need a month to ramp up.

similar.example: Let's warm up with a quick round of introductions.
The café plans to scale up once the second location opens.

expressions.quote: I'm a huge fan of structure in all communication
expressions.meaning_ko: ~을 아주 좋아하고 지지하다 (사람뿐 아니라 방식·원칙에도 사용)
expressions.nuance_ko: 취향뿐 아니라 방식이나 원칙에 대한 강한 지지를 표현할 때 쓴다. 'I'm a big fan of ~ing'로 의견을 부드럽지만 분명하게 밝힐 수 있다. 반대는 'I'm not a big fan of'로 완곡하게 거절할 때 좋다.
examples: I'm a huge fan of short stand-ups; anything longer loses people.
I'm not a big fan of back-to-back calls. I never get time to think.
She's a huge fan of walking meetings, especially when the weather's nice.

similar.example: I'm all for working from home, as long as we meet in person once a month.
I swear by writing a to-do list the night before.

expressions.quote: We don't have to fall victim to the way calendars schedule timing of meetings
expressions.nuance_ko: 범죄·사기뿐 아니라 습관이나 시스템의 함정에 빠지는 상황에도 쓴다. 부정문으로 'don't have to fall victim to...'라 하면 '굳이 거기에 휘둘릴 필요 없다'는 설득이 된다.
examples: Don't fall victim to the idea that you have to answer every message immediately.
A lot of travelers fall victim to overpriced airport taxis.
Teams often fall victim to their own default settings.

similar.expression: get caught in the trap of
similar.example: It's easy to get caught in the trap of saying yes to everything.
We're at the mercy of the weather on this trip.

expressions.expression: it's in your best interest to
expressions.quote: It is in your best interest to start on time
expressions.nuance_ko: 상대에게 조언이나 경고를 할 때 쓰는 다소 격식 있는 표현이다. 강하게 말하면 위협처럼 들릴 수 있으니 톤에 주의한다. 'in your own best interest', 'in everyone's best interest'로도 쓴다.
examples: It's in your best interest to read the contract before you sign.
It's in everyone's best interest to keep this discussion calm.
If you want the job, it's in your best interest to follow up this week.

similar.example: It'd be wise to book your flights early.
You'd do well to double-check the address.

expressions.quote: It sends a signal that we start on time
expressions.nuance_ko: 말하지 않아도 행동이 전달하는 메시지를 설명할 때 유용하다. 뒤에 that절이나 'to + 대상'을 붙인다. 정치·시장 뉴스에서도 흔하다.
examples: Replying at midnight sends a signal that you're always available.
The new policy sends a signal to employees that results matter more than hours.
Skipping the intro sends a signal that you don't care about the group.

similar.example: Cancelling at the last minute sends a message that their time doesn't matter.
A messy slide conveys the impression that you rushed.

expressions.quote: a quick and dirty thing you can do if you're leading a meeting
expressions.nuance_ko: 정교함보다 속도와 실용성을 강조한다. 말하는 사람이 겸손하게 '대충이지만 먹히는 팁'을 소개할 때 좋다. 지나치게 부정적으로 쓰면 '날림'이라는 뜻이 된다.
examples: Here's a quick and dirty way to check if a restaurant is any good: look at how busy it is at 8 p.m.
I made a quick and dirty budget in a spreadsheet just to see if we could afford the trip.
It's a quick and dirty fix, but it'll hold until the weekend.

similar.example: It's a rough and ready draft, but you'll get the idea.
Based on a back-of-the-envelope estimate, it'd take about three weeks.

expressions.quote: a side conversation that those of us in the room aren't privy to
expressions.meaning_ko: (비공개 정보 등을) 알고 있는, 접근 권한이 있는
expressions.nuance_ko: 일부만 아는 정보나 대화에 쓰는 격식 있는 표현이다. 'privy to the details/discussions'로 자주 쓰고, 부정형은 '나는 그 이야기에서 배제됐다'는 뜻이 된다.
examples: I wasn't privy to the early talks, so I can't say why they changed course.
Only a few people were privy to the plan before the announcement.
Were you privy to what they discussed at dinner?

similar.example: Keep me in the loop on the schedule.
Were you in on the surprise party?

expressions.nuance_ko: 도입을 길게 끌지 않고 본론으로 들어갈 때 쓴다. 'jump in'은 대화에 끼어들다는 뜻도 있어서 문맥으로 구분한다. 'dive right in'과 거의 같다.
examples: Let's skip the small talk and jump right in.
When I moved abroad, I just jumped right in and joined a local football club.
The workshop was great; we jumped right in with a hands-on exercise.

similar.example: I'll dive in with the budget numbers first.
Let me get straight to the point: we're running late.

expressions.quote: Many of us have an allergy to the word meeting
expressions.nuance_ko: 특정 단어, 활동, 분위기에 대한 본능적 거부감을 유머러스하게 표현한다. 'allergic to'의 비유로도 많이 쓴다. 가벼운 농담조라 친근한 자리에서 잘 어울린다.
examples: My team has an allergy to long email threads, so I just call them.
He's allergic to small talk; he always goes straight to business.
A lot of people have an allergy to the word 'networking'.

similar.example: She's averse to taking big risks.
I can't stand last-minute schedule changes.

expressions.expression: it might serve you well to
expressions.quote: It might serve you well to spend a few minutes
expressions.nuance_ko: 직접적인 지시 대신 완곡하게 조언할 때 쓰는 표현이다. 'might'로 부드럽게 만들어 상대를 압박하지 않는다. 'serve someone well'은 '유용하게 작용하다'는 뜻이다.
examples: It might serve you well to arrive early and look around the venue.
That habit will serve you well when you start managing people.
It might serve you well to ask a couple of questions before you accept.

similar.example: It wouldn't hurt to bring a spare charger.
You might want to leave earlier; traffic's bad.

vocab.example: The committee will convene on Tuesday to review the proposals.
We spent the afternoon ideating names for the new product.
It's a nice idea, but how do we operationalize it by next month?
Without a clear owner, projects tend to drift toward entropy.
The gym in our building is seriously underutilized.
Keeping your inbox under control takes constant vigilance.
She solicited feedback from everyone before finalizing the plan.
Could you itemize the expenses so I can see where the money went?
He's been honing his pitch for months.

warmup.q: Think of the worst meeting you've ever attended. What went wrong, and what would have saved it?
warmup.hint_ko: 구체적인 상황(목적 불명, 인원 과다, 시간 초과)을 하나 골라 말하고, 어떻게 고칠 수 있었을지 한두 가지 제안한다.

warmup.q: How do you usually react when a meeting gets canceled? Why do you think we feel that way?
warmup.hint_ko: 솔직한 반응과 그 이유(업무 부담, 의미 없는 회의 경험)를 말하고, 회의 문화에 대한 생각으로 연결한다.

opinion.q: Matt says to ask 'Do we really need this meeting?' before anything else. What kinds of things should never be a meeting, and what should always be one?
opinion.hint_ko: 단순 업데이트 vs 의사결정·브레인스토밍·갈등 조율 같은 기준을 세우고, 자신의 경험 사례를 한 가지 든다.

opinion.q: He suggests renaming meetings with an action, like the decision to be made. Would that work in your workplace culture?
opinion.hint_ko: 제목이 기대치를 바꾸는 효과, 문화적 저항이나 어색함, 직접 쓴다면 어떤 제목을 쓸지 말한다.

opinion.q: How should a leader make sure remote participants aren't forgotten in a hybrid meeting?
opinion.hint_ko: 소수 그룹부터 발언시키기, 채팅 제한 같은 방법에 자신의 아이디어(카메라 규칙, 발언 순서)를 더한다.

debate.q: Should companies set a default of 20- or 50-minute meetings instead of 30 or 60 minutes?
debate.for: 시간을 줄이면 집중도와 효율이 올라가고, 회의 사이에 이동·휴식 시간이 생긴다. 불필요한 잡담과 늘어짐도 막을 수 있다.
debate.against: 복잡한 안건은 오히려 쫓기게 되어 토론의 질이 떨어지고, 소수 의견을 말할 시간이 사라질 수 있다. 일괄 기본값은 상황별 유연성을 해친다.

debate.q: Should people who show up late be made to catch up on their own, even if it disrupts the flow?
debate.for: 정시 시작은 존중의 규범을 세우고, 지각자를 위해 요약해 주면 지각을 부추기게 된다. 시간 약속이 지켜지는 문화가 만들어진다.
debate.against: 불가피한 사정이 있을 수 있고, 핵심 인물이 빠지면 결정의 질이 떨어진다. 엄격한 규칙은 팀 분위기를 해칠 수 있다.

roleplay.scenario: Your team has a weekly one-hour status meeting that most people find pointless. You meet your manager for coffee to propose redesigning it.
roleplay.your_role: A team member who wants to make the meeting more effective
roleplay.partner_role: A skeptical manager who likes the current meeting and worries about losing visibility
goals: Argue that updates could be shared another way, using expressions like 'band-aid', 'fall victim to', or 'it's in everyone's best interest'.
Propose a concrete structure: goal, agenda with owners and timings, a shorter slot, and a clear wrap-up.
Handle the manager's objection and agree on a trial period with a feedback check.

useful_phrases.phrase: Do we actually need a meeting for this?
What's the outcome we're after: a decision, information, or discussion?
useful_phrases.ko: 우리가 원하는 결과가 결정인가요, 정보 공유인가요, 토론인가요?

useful_phrases.phrase: Let's wrap up by going over the action items.
It might serve us well to keep this to twenty minutes.
useful_phrases.ko: 20분으로 제한하는 게 도움이 될 것 같아요.

useful_phrases.phrase: Let me make sure the folks on Zoom have a chance to weigh in first.
useful_phrases.ko: 줌 참석자분들이 먼저 의견을 낼 기회를 드릴게요.

shadowing.reason_ko: 사례를 들어 문제 → 원인 → 결과를 짧게 풀어내는 구조가 좋고, 'band-aids'와 'brought in' 같은 표현이 자연스럽게 나온다.
'It is in your best interest', 'sends a signal' 등 설득력 있는 논리 표현이 연속해 나오며, 단호하지만 부드러운 톤을 연습하기 좋다.
'Do you know...?' 식의 질문 뒤 구체적인 마무리 멘트(감사, 목표 재확인, 액션 스텝)를 나열하는 흐름이 실전 회의에 바로 쓸 만하다.

difficulty.note_ko: 속도는 보통이고 문장이 명료한 편이다. 다만 operationalize, entropy, vigilance 같은 비즈니스·학술 어휘와 'quick and dirty', 'privy to' 같은 관용 표현이 섞여 있어 C1 수준에 맞는다.

translations_sent.0-0: 회의가 캘린더에서 취소됐을 때 느끼는 그 기쁨과 안도감, 아시죠?
translations_sent.3-3: 저는 맷 에이브러햄스이고, 스탠퍼드 경영대학원에서 전략적 커뮤니케이션을 가르치고 있습니다.
translations_sent.4-4: 팟캐스트 '싱크 패스트, 토크 스마트'의 퀵 싱크스 에피소드에 오신 것을 환영합니다.
translations_sent.5-5: 저는 회의를 어떻게 더 좋게 만들 수 있냐는 질문을 자주 받습니다.
translations_sent.6-6: 그래서 오늘은 회의를 개선해서 회의 중에도, 끝난 뒤에도 긍정적인 경험과 결과를 얻으려면 무엇을 할 수 있는지 말씀드리려고 해요.
translations_sent.7-7: 회의를 계획할 때는 세 단계, 즉 회의 전, 회의 중, 회의 후에 우리가 무엇을 하는지를 생각해야 합니다.
translations_sent.8-8: 회의와 관련해서 가장 먼저 해야 할 일은 스스로에게 "이게 정말 필요한 회의인가?"라고 묻는 겁니다.
translations_sent.9-9: 회의는 흔히 임시방편으로, 다른 더 큰 소통 문제를 덮는 수단으로 쓰입니다.
translations_sent.10-10: 한번은 대부분의 사람들이 하루에 최소 세 번씩 회의를 하는 조직에 컨설팅을 하러 간 적이 있는데, 그 회의마다 20명, 30명이 모이고 있었어요.
translations_sent.12-12: 고위 리더들의 결정과 생각을 전달할 효과적인 방법이 없었던 겁니다.
translations_sent.13-13: 그런 방법을 만들자마자 회의 수가 갑자기 사라졌어요.
translations_sent.18-18: 의사결정, 아이디어 도출 등 사람들을 모아야 할 이유는 많죠.
translations_sent.19-19: 하지만 우리가 하는 일 중에는 굳이 사람들을 모을 필요가 없는 것도 많습니다.
translations_sent.21-21: 모두가 회의실이나 줌에 앉아 있지 않아도 사람들에게 업데이트를 전할 창의적인 방법은 많습니다.
translations_sent.23-23: 회의가 필요하다고 결정했다면, 가장 큰 차원에서 그 회의의 명확한 목표가 무엇인지 생각해야 합니다.
translations_sent.24-24: 제 이야기를 전에 들어보셨다면 아시겠지만, 저는 목표에 세 부분이 있다고 믿습니다. 알기, 느끼기, 행동하기죠.
translations_sent.25-25: 회의의 결과로 사람들이 무엇을 알게 되길 원하시나요?
translations_sent.28-28: 다음 단계를 위해 이걸 명확하게 말할 수 있어야 해요. 다음 단계는 그 목표를 어떻게 실행으로 옮길지 생각하는 것이니까요.
translations_sent.29-29: 안건 목록, 즉 아젠다를 만들어야 합니다.
translations_sent.30-30: 저는 모든 커뮤니케이션에서 구조를 아주 중요하게 생각합니다.
translations_sent.32-32: 제가 보기에 좋은 아젠다에는 몇 가지 요소가 있습니다.
translations_sent.37-37: 이렇게 하면 일정한 경계를 세우는 데 도움이 됩니다.
translations_sent.38-38: 그리고 그 안건의 결과로 무엇이 이루어질지도 정해야 합니다.
translations_sent.41-41: 주제가 무엇인지, 시간을 얼마나 쓸지, 누가 맡는지, 결과물이 무엇인지 미리 알려주면 사람들이 더 잘 준비할 수 있습니다.
translations_sent.42-42: 그다음에는 안건의 순서를 어떻게 할지 생각해야 합니다.
translations_sent.43-43: 이에 대해 흥미로운 연구가 실제로 있어요.
translations_sent.44-44: 우리 대부분은 워밍업 삼아 가장 쉬운 걸 먼저 놓는 경향이 있습니다.
translations_sent.45-45: 그런데 안타깝게도 회의에는 '시간 엔트로피'라는 개념이 있어요.
translations_sent.46-46: 우리는 필요한 것보다 시간을 더 늘려 쓰는 경향이 있습니다.
translations_sent.47-47: 그래서 간단한 일에 시간을 더 쓰면, 더 어렵고 복잡한 일에 쓸 시간이 줄어듭니다.
translations_sent.48-48: 그래서 연구가 시사하는 바는, 쉬운 주제, 중간 정도 난이도의 주제, 정말 어려운 주제 이렇게 세 가지가 있다면요.
translations_sent.49-49: 중간 난이도를 먼저 두고, 그다음 가장 어려운 것으로 넘어가고, 가장 쉬운 걸로 마무리하라는 겁니다.
translations_sent.50-50: 그러니 안건이 무엇인지뿐 아니라 그 항목들이 나오는 순서까지 잘 생각해 보세요.
translations_sent.52-52: 마지막으로, 누가 회의에 참석하는지 생각해야 합니다.
translations_sent.53-53: 누구를 초대하고 누구를 필수로 지정하느냐가 정말 큰 차이를 만듭니다.
translations_sent.55-55: 그리고 사람들의 시간을 존중해야 하니까, 꼭 필요한 사람만 초대하세요.
translations_sent.56-56: 물론 회의 결과를 통보받아야 하는 사람들이 있을 수도 있습니다.
translations_sent.57-57: 그건 괜찮아요. 그들을 회의에 초대하지는 마세요.
translations_sent.58-58: 심지어 이분들이 회의 결과물을 받을 사람들이라고 적어두는 것도 좋아요.
translations_sent.59-59: 이렇게 미리 계획하면 회의가 효과적일 가능성이 높아지고, 사람들도 거기에 가치가 있다고 존중하게 됩니다.
translations_sent.61-61: 목표가 뭔가?' 하고 생각하는 것부터 시작합니다.
translations_sent.64-64: 실제로 회의를 하기 전의 다음 단계는 회의를 공지하는 겁니다.
translations_sent.65-65: 특히 회의와 발표에서 우리가 가진 기대치 설정 도구 중 가장 활용이 덜 되는 것 하나가 캘린더 초대라고 생각해요.
translations_sent.67-67: 행동이 담긴 회의여야 하는 게 중요합니다.
translations_sent.68-68: 우리 중 많은 사람이 '회의'라는 단어에 알레르기가 있으니, 모임을 회의라고 부르지 마세요.
translations_sent.71-71: 내려야 할 결정이나 만들어낼 아이디어를 분명히 적으세요.
translations_sent.73-73: 회의가 열리는 시간, 즉 길이와 시간대를 모두 생각해야 합니다.
translations_sent.76-76: 그리고 참고로 회의가 꼭 30분이나 한 시간일 필요는 없습니다.
translations_sent.78-78: 캘린더가 회의 시간을 정해 주는 방식에 끌려갈 필요는 없습니다.

translations_sent.109-109: 하지만 모든 사람이 원할 때 의견을 낼 기회를 갖도록 하는 것도 신경 써야 합니다.
